timelineItems.text: Service by Rev. L.C. Hermerding in Muskogee & Tulsa in the Masonic Hall.
Rev. Hermerding accepts a call in Kansas. Work in Tulsa stopped for almost a decade.
Services by Rev. M. Bredehoft at Mrs. A. Randall's, later at the courthouse.
Rev. C.A. Luerssen arrives. Lot purchased at 13th & Quincy.
Frame church on 13th & Quincy dedicated.
Rev. Luerssen leaves. Pastor Karl Frese installed September 21.
Congregation organized.
Lots purchased at 5th & Lewis - $6,000.
Basement ($6,655) and parsonage ($6,390) erected - Total $13,045.
Superstructure dedicated - building ($17,013), furniture ($2,354), Kilgen organ ($3,000).
Pastor Frese's resignation accepted. Farewell sermon October 27, 1946.
Pastor Knippa installed November 24.
Church enlarged and educational wing added (dedicated 2/24/52) - $104,208 total: building ($88,000), furniture ($15,682), windows ($526).
Air conditioning ($25,183).
Stained glass in nave, transepts, and prayer room ($12,725).
Altar window ($5,274).
Moeller organ dedicated 12/5/65 and choir gallery and narthex remodeled.
Purchase of homes on lots 5, 6, 7, and 8, west parking lot provided ($48,647).
January 18 - Fire - damage $102,000, recovered $101,000. Services temporarily at St. Francis Catholic Church. April 28 - Services back in church again. Chimes added to organ.
April 13 - Construction on educational addition begun. Completed September 1, 1970.
May 31 - Pastor Knippa retires and made Pastor Emeritus. July - Pastor James R. Haner installed.
Property north of the church purchased ($40,000).
Chancel remodeled. Property north of the church sold and the southwest corner of 5th Place and Lewis purchased and a parking lot constructed.
An addition of 14,000 square feet was completed, the educational wing remodeled and an elevator installed. Knippa Hall dedicated August 29, 1999. ($1,500,000)
Dr. Kenneth Sole hired as organist and church musician; continued as Organist Emeritus until his death in 2017.
Rev. Mason T. Beecroft was installed as pastor September 11, 2005. Continued until late 2010.
Courtyard landscaped April 2008. Christian C. Tiews installed as vicar August 16, 2008.
Walt Sabourin appointed deacon February 22, 2009. Christian C. Tiews installed as associate pastor August 16, 2009; accepted a call to Trinity Lutheran, Okmulgee, November 2015.
Christopher D. Hall installed as senior pastor May 6, 2012. Marjorie Hall hired as Part-Time Parish Musician.
Marjorie Hall added Youth Coordinator responsibilities in June; hired as Full-Time Parish Musician in 2015.
Alyssa Lehenbauer hired as Youth Director; accepted a teaching position at a Lutheran academy in Missouri, August 2020.
Total renovation of the entire third floor; named the Charles Biederman Educational Wing.
Joshua Craig called as Director of Christian Education.

sections.heading: Historic Lutheran Pastors
sections.body:
The beginning of the 20th century found Oklahoma as Indian Territory in government records and as a part of the Kansas District of the Evangelical Lutheran Synod of Missouri, Ohio and other states in church records. In 1906 the Kansas District sent the Rev. L. C. Hermerding to Muskogee to serve Lutherans in the Territory. On his exploratory trips, he came to Tulsa and gave pastoral service to a few Lutherans who were members of the General Synod and held services once a month in the Masonic Hall. In the fall of 1907, he accepted a call to a station in Kansas, and the work in Tulsa stopped for almost a decade.

Work in Tulsa was resumed in 1917 when the Kansas District requested the Rev. M. Bredehoeft of Broken Arrow to serve the Lutherans in Tulsa. His first service was conducted in the home of Mrs. A. Randall, followed by later services in the court house.

The Rev. C. Luerssen, the first resident pastor and a recent seminary graduate, came to Tulsa in August, 1919. Within 18 months a frame chapel was built at 13th & Quincy and dedicated on the first Sunday in January, 1921, with the speakers being the Rev. K. Frese of Shawnee and the Rev. A.C. Dubberstein of Oklahoma City. The following July, the Rev. Luerssen accepted a call to Baltimore.

After the departure of Rev. Luerssen, The Kansas District extended a call to the Rev. K. Frese, who was installed on the second Sunday in September 1921, by the Rev. Erwin Umbach of Muskogee. Less than six months after Pastor Frese arrived, the congregation was formally organized on February 1, 1922. The original members signing the instrument of organization were: Rev. Karl Frese, Walter H. Goller, Louis Miller, H.G. Biederman, Gustav Hartman, August Gilbert Rasch, George Emmert, Paul Heinritz, Fred Schuette.

In the meeting of February 15, 1922, the following became the first elected officers: Chairman – G. Hartman, Elders – G. Hartman and L. Miller, Secretary-Treasurer – John Roehling, Auditors – H.G. Biederman and W. H. Goller.

In 1924, the Oklahoma District was organized at Okarche, and Grace Church was among the charter members. Grace Church continued to receive a subsidy from the Oklahoma District until July 1, 1928, when it became self-sustaining.

During 1928 Grace purchased vacant lots at its present location for an approximate cost of $6,000. Almost within a year, the basement unit of a proposed church building was completed with tile walls and buff brick veneer at an approximate cost of $6,500. Concurrently, the adjoining parsonage was completed with the same type of brick veneer at an approximate cost of $5,500. The cost of the lots and the basement church were financed with a loan from the Church Extension Fund, while the cost of the parsonage was financed with a commercial loan.

In August 1929, the congregation was incorporated under the laws of Oklahoma as Grace Evangelical Lutheran Church of Tulsa, Oklahoma.

The joy at the dedication of the church on September 8, 1929, was unmarred by foreboding of the impending national depression which within only a few weeks was ushered in with a disastrous collapse of stock prices on Wall Street. Grace Church was not spared the severe financial problems and other hardships widely associated with the depression. For over a decade it was delayed in completing the superstructure, and during this time the basement was adapted to serve for all church functions.

Finally on June 21, 1941, work got underway again when ground was broken for the erection of the complete unit. However, the design of the original plan was abandoned, and a new plan was adopted designed after the English Parish Church of the 14th and 15th centuries. The brick walls were removed, and the building was erected out of native limestone. It was completed at a cost of approximately $18,500 including furnishings. The dedication took place on December 21, 1941, and the speakers were Dr. J. W. Behnken, President of Synod; the Rev. E. Hauer, President of the Oklahoma District; and the Rev. L.O. Streufert, Secretary of Missions. During construction, services were conducted at the Circle Theatre.

Grace members were saddened when health issues occurred following a heart attack. Pastor Frese resigned his pastorate after 25 years of faithful service. On October 27, 1946, at a farewell service, the congregation conferred upon Pastor Frese the title of Pastor Emeritus and gave him a gift to retire the debt on a house he had purchased. Pastor Frese continued his membership at Grace Church until his death – November 14, 1955.

The Rev. Clarence W. Knippa of Houston, Texas, was installed as pastor on November 24, 1946. Pastor Frese performed the installation rites. The Rev. Walmer W. Frank of The Lutheran Church of the Good Shepherd in Tulsa preached the sermon.

Grace Church celebrated its 25th anniversary in 1947 during the week commencing February 23. Dr. J. W. Behnken, President of Synod, spoke at the first Sunday service, which was designated a Service of Thanksgiving. Pastor Frese spoke in the evening Youth Service; Prof. Lorenz Wunderlich of St. John's College spoke on Wednesday evening at the Service of Missions; Pastor Knippa spoke on Thursday evening at the Service of Music; Pastor Walmar Frank spoke at the fellowship dinner on Friday evening; and Pastor Knippa spoke at the service of Rededication on Sunday, March 2nd. At the time of this event, the population of Tulsa was 180,000 and Grace Church numbered 475 souls.

The building was enlarged in 1951 by the addition of a chancel area, transepts, and education wing, a foyer and west porch. New lighting fixtures were installed in the nave. The cost was approximately $88,000, and the cost of additional furniture was $15,682. The enlarged church was dedicated on February 24, 1951, and the speakers were the Rev. Oliver R. Harms of Houston and the Rev. George Hoyer of Topeka. During construction, services were conducted at the Royal Theatre.

In 1956, the spire, rising seventy-five feet above street level and crested with a cross, was placed on the church. (In the spring of 2018, the wooden base of the steeple had rotted. During repairs, the steeple received a new sheathing of copper as well. Today the bell tower continues to toll and is accompanied by a hymn). In 1957 air conditioning was installed at a cost of $25,180. The installation of stained glass in all windows was completed in February, 1958. These windows, designed by A. R. Kretzmann, in the nave symbolize God's promise of a Savior, while the transepts and chancel windows are dedicated to the life of our Lord. The two small windows in the prayer room on one side of the chancel area represent Peter and Paul. Many of the windows were gifts from members as memorials.

Early in 1965, a planning and resources committee was formed to review the mission and ministry of Grace Church, its location and facilities, its opportunities and limitations. A long-range and a short-range plan was devised including the improvement of congregational worship by the installation of an organ, acquisition of land for expansion of the educational wing and the parking area, the erection of needed education and youth, and an emphasis on community ministry. Priorities were set and action was taken to provide the funds needed to implement these plans.

During the year 1965, a new 16 rank Moeller pipe organ which cost approximately $30,000 was installed to replace the old Kilgen organ. The Kilgen had been installed during the war years as a reconditioned theatre organ. Along with the installation of the new organ, the choir gallery and narthex were enlarged.

To provide for additional parking space, four lots including three homes were purchased in 1966 at a cost of $48,647. All of the houses on these lots were removed except an apartment house on the corner lot.

On the morning of January 18, 1968, radio bulletins broke the shocking news that during the night a disastrous fire had severely damaged Grace Lutheran Church. A complete destruction of the building had been narrowly averted when by chance a neighbor had noticed smoke coming from the building. Her call brought a quick response by the fire department which arrived just in time to subdue the flames before it broke through the roof. The damage was $103,000 but was well covered by insurance. Immediately offers were received from St. Francis Catholic Church, First Lutheran Church and others for the use of their churches. During the reconstruction period of three months, Sunday services were conducted at St. Francis while evening Lenten services and other meetings were conducted at First Lutheran. Good Friday services were held at College Hill Presbyterian Church. A new Moeller organ was installed to replace the one seriously damaged, and chimes were added as the gift of an anonymous donor. An electronic carillon was not replaced. Services were resumed at Grace Church on April 28, 1968.

Grace Church was again enlarged in 1970 by an addition to the education wing at an approximate cost of $95,000. The former parsonage was remodeled into a youth center. A portion of the cost was financed through the sale of bonds.

Grace Church joined churches of other denominations in 1970 in providing a summer program for children in the neighborhood and a program of tutoring during the school year. The program, Kendall Whittier, Inc., continues today.

Attempting to keep an appropriate balance between program, staff and facilities, the congregation decided that the time had arrived when the office of Minister of Education and Youth should be activated. A call was extended to the Rev. John C. Zeile, who had previously vacated at Grace, and who was completing his studies at Concordia Seminary, St. Louis. Pastor Zeile accepted the call and was installed as Minister of Education & Youth on June 27, 1971. Pastor Knippa preached the sermon and the rite of installation was performed by the Rev. Harold A. Brockhoff, President of the Oklahoma District. Weekday Bible School was expanded in the fall to include classes for all ages and is a major agency of Christian education in the congregation.

A special service of celebration on December 5, 1971, acknowledged twenty-five years of service by Pastor Knippa to Grace Church, and also acknowledged his thirty-fifth anniversary of ordination into the Holy Ministry. The Rev. Walmar Frank delivered the sermon, and Pastor Zeile was the liturgist. In appreciation of Pastor Knippa's 25 years of faithful service, the congregation arranged to establish a fund for a trip to the Holy Land for Pastor & Mrs. Knippa.

On January 16, 1972, the congregation gratefully received as a gift from Pastor & Mrs. Knippa a life-sized statue of Martin Luther. Orren Jerome Sahlman was the artist who carved this fine statue out of pecan wood. Authentic in detail, this statue depicts Luther as resolute and dedicated, but in virile kindness expounding the grace of God in Christ. The statue was placed on a pedestal immediately overlooking the pulpit. Mr. Sahlman's next work was the statue of St. Paul which was placed on a pedestal overlooking the lectern.

sections.heading: Buildings of Worship
sections.body:
The Rev. M. Bredehoeft of Broken Arrow served Lutherans in Tulsa at the home of Mrs. A. Randall. Rev. Bredehoeft (who was also a dairy farmer) was the father of Gertrude McCoy.

The Rev. C. Luerssen, the first resident pastor and a recent seminary graduate, came to Tulsa in August 1919. Within 18 months a frame chapel was built at 13th and Quincy and was dedicated in January 1921.

sections.heading: Parsonage
sections.body:
The parsonage was used by Pastor Knippa and his family during the 40's. It was located just west of our courtyard. Today our church offices occupy that spot. Its exterior matched the original buff colored brick on the basement church. The parsonage sported two bedrooms and a study. Today we are amazed that Pastor and Elsie raised 5 children in that small home. After Pastor and his family moved to larger accommodations, over the years the house served as headquarters to various groups: a youth hall, an office of Kendall Whittier Ministry, and Meals-On-Wheels facility.

It was torn down in 1999 when the 14,000 square foot wing was added which houses Knippa Hall, Sunday School rooms & nursery, Haner Conference Room, music room, kitchen, choir room, and staff offices.

sections.heading: Grace Damaged by Fire
sections.body:
Excerpt from March 1968 Lutheran Witness

Tulsa Church Damaged by Fire

Damage was $100,000, but no one was hurt in the 2AM fire at Grace Church, Tulsa, on Jan 18, 1968. Pastor Clarence Knippa arrived at the burning church in time to warn firemen about the value of its 20 stained glass windows. Erected in 1941 and enlarged in 1952 to 80 by 32 feet, the church is of stone construction with a roof of 3-inch-thick planks. The roof was charred but did not burn through. A 15-rank Moller pipe organ, less than 2 years old, was completely destroyed by the heat, as was much of the interior furnishings and equipment. The chancel area suffered especially heavy damage.

Beginning in a basement choir-music storage room, the fire had about an hour's headway before it was discovered by neighbors and passing policemen. Firemen awakened Vicar Roger Kuehn, whose apartment is next to the church. Pastor Knippa had high praise for the firemen, who needed oxygen to enter the smoke-filled building and had to come out several times for fresh air. Immediate offers of aid came from nearby churches of several denominations. The congregation accepted the plan to hold Sunday services in the nave of St. Francis Xavier Catholic Church and to use that church's parochial school buildings, now vacant, for Sunday school sessions. Weekday activities are being held in the facilities of First Lutheran, an LCA congregation not far from Grace Church.

Cleanup operations in the parish hall, Pastor Knippa said, will require less time than restoring the church nave and basement, which were most heavily damaged.

sections.heading: Naves of the Church & Original Windows
sections.body: The three beautiful stained glass windows that were originally above the altar were replaced when the current chancel window was installed. They were reconfigured with the top half of each window being installed in the narthex, and the bottom half placed in the choir loft.

sideImages.caption: The 3 windows as they appear today on the south wall of the narthex.

sections.heading: Pastors of Grace
sections.body:
In the long hallway between Knippa Hall and the church office we have a gallery of photographs displaying our pastors here at Grace.

Rev. Luerssen, the first resident pastor came to Tulsa in August 1919. Within 18 months a frame chapel was built at 13th and Quincy and Pastor Luerssen served until July of 1921. Pastor Frese came in September of 1921. On February 1, 1922, Grace was formally organized with a charter. The tenure is as follows: Pastor Luerssen 1919-1921; Pastor Frese 1921-1946; Pastor Knippa 1946-1979; Pastor Haner 1979-2005; Pastor Beecroft 2005-2011; Assoc. Pastor Christian C. Tiews 2009 to present; Senior Pastor Christopher D. Hall 2012 to present.

However, there were pastors who served Lutherans in Oklahoma before 1921. Before statehood in 1906, the Kansas District sent Rev. L. C. Hermerding to Muskogee to serve Lutherans in the Oklahoma Territory. On his exploratory trips, he came to Tulsa and gave pastoral service to a few Lutherans who were members of the General Synod. He held services once a month in the Masonic Hall. In the fall of 1907, he accepted a call to a station in Kansas and the work in Tulsa stopped for almost a decade. Pastor Bredehoeft of Broken Arrow served in 1917. Rev. Luerssen, the first resident pastor came to Tulsa in August 1919.
